feedback: If a learner appends zeros to a decimal (3.45×100 → 3.4500): on the chart, multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100× more, so each digit moves two columns left — the '3' becomes 3 hundreds. The point does not move; the digits do. The correct answer is 345.

If 72÷1000 comes out as 720 or 7.2: dividing makes each digit worth a thousandth as much, so the digits move exactly three columns to the RIGHT. 720 has moved them left (the wrong direction), and 7.2 has moved them only one place right instead of three.
If 72÷1000 is written as 0.72 (too few decimal places): count every column each digit crosses and drop a zero into each empty one so 72 lands correctly as 0.072.

If the place count is off by one under speed: this may be a counting slip rather than a misunderstanding. Recount the zeros in 10/100/1000, match them to the places shifted, and check whether the error comes back on similar items.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying or dividing by a power of ten changes what each digit is worth, so the digits shift the matching number of place-value columns; the decimal point does not move, and empty columns must be filled with placeholder zeros.
learnerActions: Set up a place-value chart with labelled columns from hundreds down to thousandths (… H  T  O • t  h  th) and a fixed decimal point.
Place 3.45 in the columns, then multiply by 100: slide every digit TWO columns to the LEFT so the 3, 4 and 5 become 345. Note that nothing was appended — the digits moved.
Now test the tempting 'just add two zeros' shortcut on 3.45 and compare: it gives 3.4500, which is wrong. Discuss why the shortcut fails for decimals.
Divide 72 by 1000: slide every digit THREE columns to the RIGHT, and fill each empty column it crosses with a placeholder zero, giving 0.072 (including the leading 0).
Compute 6 × 10 by sliding one place left (giving 60), and connect the number of places shifted to the number of zeros in 10/100/1000 (×1000 → 3 places).
Optionally switch the chart to a metric mode so the same kind of shift is reread as a conversion: metres → centimetres is ×100 (two places left) and centimetres → millimetres is ×10 (one place left).
activities.title: Sliding digits on a place-value chart

feedback: For the 3.45×100 choice: 3.4500 keeps the point fixed and tacks on zeros, leaving the value unchanged — wrong. Sliding each digit two places left gives 345.
For 72÷1000: a missing placeholder zero gives 0.72; count the crossed columns to reach 0.072.
An off-by-one place error may be a counting slip, so recount and see whether it happens again; a wrong direction signals the digit-shift idea needs revisiting.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidation surfaces the specific decimal trap (3.4500) and the placeholder-zero requirement (0.072), confirming whether digit-shift reasoning is secure rather than a fragile trick.
learnerActions: Choose the correct value of 3.45 × 100 from options including the trap value 3.4500, and explain why the trap is wrong.
Find and fix the mistake in a worked example where a digit has been shifted the wrong number of places.
Explain, for one of your answers, how the value of each digit changed.
activities.title: Spot-the-error and fill-in consolidation

feedback: If the learner defends 'add a zero': ask what each digit is now worth — in 345 the 3 is 3 hundreds, so the digits moved, they were not padded.
If they are unsure how to express it: 'multiplying by 100 makes every digit worth 100 times more, so each slides two columns left.'
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating why 'add a zero' works for whole numbers but fails for decimals turns a half-learned rule into reasoned understanding of the digit shift.
learnerActions: Respond to a character who insists you can always 'just add a zero' to multiply by ten.
Test the claim on a whole number (6 × 10 = 60) where it seems to work, then on a decimal (3.45 × 100) where it produces 3.4500.
Argue, using place value, why the claim is unsafe and what actually happens to the digits.
activities.title: Testing the 'just add a zero' claim out loud
